newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bankers slightly disappointed with Basle Committee.
newsitem.headline: Bankers slightly disappointed with Basle Committee.

text.p: Private bankers are sympathetic to the prudent approach taken by the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision but remain slightly disappointed that supervisors will still require them to use a multiplier of minimum three when calculating capital charges.

Mark Wallace, managing director of risk control at Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) and board member of the International Swaps and Derivatives Dealers Association (ISDA), said the multiplier was too high and not flexible enough to differentiate between banks that have superior risk controls and those that do not.
"We are not taking issue with the multiplier, but we think it's too high and there is not enough of a range," Wallace told Reuters in response to inquiries.
Wallace was reacting to a decision by the Basle Committee published today to retain a multiplication factor of three times the outcome of value-at-risk (VaR) calculations.

Private bankers have been critical of the size of the multiplicator ever since the Basle Committee first aired its proposal last year to amend the 1988 Capital Accord to include market risks in addition to credit risks.
The amendment to the Capital Accord was approved by G10 central bank governors in December 1995 and will take effect by the end of 1997, at the latest.
The amendment broke new regulatory ground by allowing banks for the first time to use their own VaR models as an alternative to the traditional, standardised framework for measuring risks.

But in order to use their internal models, banks must fulfill strict quantitative and qualitative standards, including multiplying the banks' exposure, as calculated by its own models, by a minium of three.

The Basle Committee said tests based on the actual portfolios of major banks had showed the capital charge in fact was less when banks use the internal model -- including the multiplier -- compared with the cruder, standardised model.
Wallace agreed it was a step forward that banks were allowed to use their own models, but he hoped the Basle Committee would continue to reconsider the size of the multiplier.

Wallace, who is also chairman of the ISDA-LIBA joint models' task force, said the multiplier should be applied in flexible manner -- for example between two and five -- to act as an incentive for banks to improve their risk management practices.
LIBA -- The London Investment Banking Association -- and ISDA formed the task force to work with the Basle Committee on specific risks and back testing.
"In relative terms it is worth for banks to use their own models, but the absolute amount of capital still has little relation to the relative risk in the portfolio," Wallace said.

Wallace also welcomed that the Basle Committee had expressed its encouragement with progress by banks in modelling specific risk -- the risk that a bank's position in a portfolio moves more or less than the general market.
"We are encouraged by the statement and look forward to providing evidence of the models," Wallace said.

While the Basle Committee said it was encouraged by the industry's progress in modelling such risks, it is not yet convinced that existing models can capture all risk elements and would retain its current specific-risk charges.
The committee said it was ready to review this promptly if and when the industry could provide convincing evidence that specific risks were adequately modelled.
